newsitem.title: USA: Disney signs Eisner to long-term pact, reveals Ovitz' pay.
newsitem.headline: Disney signs Eisner to long-term pact, reveals Ovitz' pay.

text.p: Walt Disney Co. Thursday signed Chairman Michael Eisner to a 10-year contract and said former President Michael Ovitz received a cash-and-stock severance package that could be worth nearly $140 million.

According to the company's annual proxy statement, Ovitz, who left Disney last month, received $38.9 million in cash and a stock option for 3 million shares of Disney stock. Based on Disney's current share price of $67.50, the options are worth $31.5 million.

But if Disney's stock rises an average of 5 percent a year until 2002, the deadline for Ovitz to exercise the options, the options could be worth more than $100 million. The options became exercisable on Dec. 27 when Ovitz resigned.
Ovitz, widely regarded as one of the most powerful men in Hollywood, agreed to step down last month after a rocky 14 months as president of the entertainment giant.

His buyout package has come under fire from critics as excessive for the limited amount of time he spent at Disney. Last week a group of Disney shareholders filed a lawsuit to block the payout but Disney said the suit was filed too late.

Disney declined to comment on the criticism, other than to say Ovitz' compensation was part of a five-year employment contract between Ovitz and Disney and was in line with other executive agreements in Hollywood.

For 1996, Eisner received a base salary of $750,000, plus a bonus of $7.9 million, bringing his total cash compensation to $8.65 million. In addition he received options on 8 million shares at various prices.

Under the company's proposed long-term employment contract, Disney said Eisner's base salary would remain at $750,000 but his bonus would be tied to the company's financial performance. The contract runs until Sept. 30, 2006.

Disney, which operates theme parks, film studios and television and radio stations, said the bonus formula is tied to the growth of the company's earnings per share above an annual threshold growth rate of 7.5 percent.
In a statement, Ray Watson, chairman of the executive committee of the Disney board of directors, said the new contract ties Eisner's compensation to the overall performace of the company.
"The contract follows the pattern of his two previous agreements by making rewards dependent on the company's future performance," he said.
The bonus formula for the new agreement will be submitted for stockholder approval at the company's stockholder meeting on Feb. 25.
Disney's stock closed down 62.5 cents at $67.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
